Pesach Day 1.nameMeaning: Pesach (פֶּסַח) means 'Passover', referring to God 'passing over' the houses of the Israelites during the final plague.
Pesach Day 1.context: This day commemorates the exact historical moment of liberation from Egyptian slavery. The readings are chosen to reflect the original event, the specific sacrifices of the day, and the very first Passover observed by the Israelites after entering the Land of Israel.
Pesach Day 1.summary: Main Torah Reading (Exodus 12:21-51): Details the original Passover night in Egypt, the smearing of the blood on the doorposts, the Plague of the Firstborn, and the Exodus itself. Maftir (Numbers 28:16-25): Describes the specific holiday sacrifices brought in the Temple. Haftarah (Joshua 3:5-7; 5:2-6:1; 6:27): Recounts how Joshua circumcised the new generation of Israelites and celebrated the first Passover after crossing the Jordan River into the Promised Land.
Pesach Day 1.significance: Each reading plays a crucial role. The main Torah reading grounds us in the visceral, historical memory of our liberation from slavery. The Maftir links us to the centralized, communal worship of the Temple era. Most profoundly, the Haftarah completes the narrative arc: while the Torah shows the *beginning* of the journey out of Egypt, the Haftarah shows the *arrival*, as the newly free generation observes Passover in the Promised Land for the very first time. Together, they teach that freedom is a journey from oppression to a purposeful life in a homeland.

Pesach Day 2.context: In the Diaspora, the second day of major festivals is observed as a full holiday (Yom Tov). It also marks the beginning of Sefirat HaOmer, the 49-day counting of the Omer leading up to Shavuot.
Pesach Day 2.summary: Main Torah Reading (Leviticus 22:26-23:44): Provides an overview of the Jewish festival cycle, specifically detailing the laws of Passover and the bringing of the Omer offering. Maftir (Numbers 28:16-25): Repeats the holiday sacrifices. Haftarah (2 Kings 23:1-9, 21-25): Describes King Josiah's massive national restoration of the Passover sacrifice after years of spiritual neglect.
Pesach Day 2.significance: This day shifts our focus from the historical Exodus to the ongoing agricultural and spiritual calendar. The Torah reading anchors us in the rhythm of the Jewish year. The Haftarah provides a powerful historical lesson on resilience: King Josiah uncovers a lost Torah scroll and realizes the nation has forgotten Passover. His passionate revival of the festival teaches that even when sacred traditions are lost or neglected by an entire generation, they can be powerfully restored.

Shabbat, Chol Hamoed, Pesach.nameMeaning: The Sabbath during the Intermediate Days of Passover.
Shabbat, Chol Hamoed, Pesach.context: When Shabbat falls during the intermediate days of a festival, the regular weekly portion is suspended in favor of a reading that highlights both the specific holiday and the sanctity of Shabbat.
Shabbat, Chol Hamoed, Pesach.summary: Main Torah Reading (Exodus 33:12-34:26): Recounts Moses pleading with God after the Golden Calf, the revelation of the 13 Attributes of Mercy, and concludes with the command to observe the three Pilgrimage Festivals. Maftir (Numbers 28:19-25): Details the daily Passover sacrifices. Haftarah (Ezekiel 37:1-14): The famous prophetic Vision of the Valley of Dry Bones.
Shabbat, Chol Hamoed, Pesach.significance: The pairing of these readings creates a profound theme of spiritual and national resurrection. In the Torah, God forgives the Israelites after their lowest point (the Golden Calf) and renews the covenant, proving that spiritual rebirth is possible. The Haftarah expands this to the national level: Ezekiel's vision of dry bones coming back to life is the ultimate promise that God will revive the exiled, hopeless nation. It connects the historical liberation of Passover with the ultimate, future Messianic redemption.

Chol Hamoed Day 1 (E\"Y 2).nameMeaning: The First Intermediate Day of Passover.
Chol Hamoed Day 1 (E\"Y 2).context: The intermediate days (Chol HaMoed) retain the sanctity of the festival but allow for certain types of work. The Torah readings for these days focus on specific commandments that serve as physical reminders of the Exodus.
Chol Hamoed Day 1 (E\"Y 2).summary: Main Torah Reading (Exodus 13:1-16): Focuses on the sanctification of the firstborn and the commandment to wear Tefillin (phylacteries). Maftir (Numbers 28:19-25): Details the daily Passover sacrifices.
Chol Hamoed Day 1 (E\"Y 2).significance: Tefillin contain scrolls that recount the Exodus story. By binding them to the arm and head, a Jew physically ties the memory of liberation to their actions (arm) and thoughts (head). This reading teaches that freedom must not merely be celebrated once a year at the Seder, but must be consciously remembered and actively applied every single day.

Chol Hamoed Day 2 (E\"Y 3).nameMeaning: The Second Intermediate Day of Passover.
Chol Hamoed Day 2 (E\"Y 3).context: The readings continue to explore how the experience of slavery and liberation should shape a just society.
Chol Hamoed Day 2 (E\"Y 3).summary: Main Torah Reading (Exodus 22:24-23:19): Discusses social justice, laws regarding ethical lending, and concludes with the commandment to observe the three Pilgrimage Festivals, reminding the people to 'never appear before God empty-handed.' Maftir (Numbers 28:19-25): Details the daily Passover sacrifices.
Chol Hamoed Day 2 (E\"Y 3).significance: The Torah directly links the Exodus to social justice. Because the Israelites were vulnerable slaves in Egypt, their new society must fiercely protect the vulnerable—the poor, the widow, and the orphan. This reading reminds us that true freedom is demonstrated by how a society treats its weakest members and how generously it approaches God.

Chol Hamoed Day 4 (E\"Y 5).nameMeaning: The Fourth Intermediate Day of Passover.
Chol Hamoed Day 4 (E\"Y 5).context: This reading addresses the human desire to participate in sacred communal acts, even when circumstances prevent it.
Chol Hamoed Day 4 (E\"Y 5).summary: Main Torah Reading (Numbers 9:1-14): Introduces 'Pesach Sheni' (the Second Passover). It tells the story of individuals who were ritually impure and missed the original Passover, prompting God to grant a makeup date one month later. Maftir (Numbers 28:19-25): Details the daily Passover sacrifices.
Chol Hamoed Day 4 (E\"Y 5).significance: Pesach Sheni is a uniquely empowering law. It was instituted not top-down by God, but bottom-up because of the passionate plea of the people ('Why should we be excluded?'). It teaches that it is never too late to correct a missed spiritual opportunity, and that God responds deeply to a genuine human desire to draw near to Him.

Shviee Shel Pesach.nameMeaning: Shvi'i Shel Pesach (שְׁבִיעִי שֶׁל פֶּסַח) means 'The Seventh Day of Passover'.
Shviee Shel Pesach.context: This day commemorates the miraculous Splitting of the Red Sea (Yam Suf), which according to tradition occurred exactly seven days after the Israelites fled Egypt.
Shviee Shel Pesach.summary: Main Torah Reading (Exodus 13:17-15:26): Recounts the dramatic Splitting of the Sea and the triumphant Song of the Sea (Az Yashir). Maftir (Numbers 28:19-25): Details the daily Passover sacrifices. Haftarah (2 Samuel 22:1-51): King David's magnificent song of deliverance.
Shviee Shel Pesach.significance: The seventh day represents the completion of physical liberation. The sea crossing was the ultimate leap of faith, requiring the Israelites to walk into the waters before they split. The Haftarah perfectly mirrors the Torah: just as Moses and the Israelites sang a song of praise after being saved from Pharaoh, King David sings a triumphant song of praise after being saved from his enemies. Together, they teach that experiencing divine salvation should naturally overflow into song, praise, and profound gratitude.

Achron Shel Pesach.nameMeaning: Acharon Shel Pesach (אַחֲרוֹן שֶׁל פֶּסַח) means 'The Last Day of Passover'.
Achron Shel Pesach.context: Observed in the Diaspora, this day concludes the Passover festival. The thematic focus dramatically shifts from the past redemption in Egypt to the future Messianic redemption.
Achron Shel Pesach.summary: Main Torah Reading (Deuteronomy 15:19-16:17): Summarizes the laws of tithing, charity, and the Pilgrimage Festivals, placing a heavy emphasis on community care. Maftir (Numbers 28:19-25): Details the daily Passover sacrifices. Haftarah (Isaiah 10:32-12:6): Describes the future Messianic era, predicting a time when 'the wolf will dwell with the lamb.'
Achron Shel Pesach.significance: By concluding Passover with Isaiah's utopian vision in the Haftarah, the holiday connects our historical origin story with our ultimate destiny. The Torah's emphasis on charity and community care teaches that the path to this peaceful Messianic future is paved by building a just, compassionate society in the present. Passover starts by looking back at Egypt, but it ends by looking forward to universal peace.

Rosh Hashanah 1.nameMeaning: Rosh Hashanah (רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה) means 'Head of the Year', the Jewish New Year.
Rosh Hashanah 1.context: As the Day of Judgment and Remembrance, the readings focus on God 'remembering' the barren, highlighting themes of divine intervention, memory, and the power of prayer.
Rosh Hashanah 1.summary: Main Torah Reading (Genesis 21:1-34): Describes the miraculous birth of Isaac after God 'remembered' Sarah. Maftir (Numbers 29:1-6): Commands the blowing of the Shofar. Haftarah (1 Samuel 1:1-2:10): Tells of Hannah's fervent, silent prayer for a child and the birth of the prophet Samuel.
Rosh Hashanah 1.significance: The Torah and Haftarah are perfectly matched: both Sarah and Hannah were barren, and both were 'remembered' by God on Rosh Hashanah after intense prayer. Their stories teach that individual, heartfelt prayer can alter destiny. The readings beautifully shift the focus of the 'New Year' from grand cosmic creation to the intimate, miraculous birth of a single child, reminding us that every human life is an entire universe.

Rosh Hashanah 2.nameMeaning: The Second Day of Rosh Hashanah.
Rosh Hashanah 2.context: The second day continues the themes of judgment and divine sovereignty, culminating in the ultimate test of faith.
Rosh Hashanah 2.summary: Main Torah Reading (Genesis 22:1-24): Recounts the Akedah (Binding of Isaac), where Abraham is commanded to sacrifice his son but is stopped by an angel, offering a ram instead. Maftir (Numbers 29:1-6): Repeats the Shofar command. Haftarah (Jeremiah 31:1-19): Features the matriarch Rachel weeping for her exiled children and God's promise of their return.
Rosh Hashanah 2.significance: The Akedah in the Torah reading is the foundational merit of the Jewish people; we blow a ram's horn (Shofar) to invoke the ram sacrificed in Isaac's place. It represents ultimate, terrifying dedication to God. However, the Haftarah balances this awe with profound maternal love. Rachel's tears move God to promise redemption for her children. Together, the day balances the terrifying awe of divine command with the comforting promise of God's unending mercy and forgiveness.

Yom Kippur.nameMeaning: Yom Kippur (יוֹם כִּפּוּר) means 'Day of Atonement'.
Yom Kippur.context: The holiest day of the year, focused entirely on fasting, repentance (Teshuvah), and seeking forgiveness from God and fellow humans.
Yom Kippur.summary: Main Torah Reading (Leviticus 16:1-34): Details the complex, awe-inspiring service of the High Priest in the Holy of Holies, including the scapegoat ritual. Maftir (Numbers 29:7-11): Details the day's sacrifices and the command to fast. Haftarah (Isaiah 57:14-58:14): A sharp prophetic critique warning that fasting without social justice is meaningless.
Yom Kippur.significance: The contrast between the Torah and Haftarah is deliberate and profound. The Torah provides the highly structured, ritual path to national atonement through the physical Temple service. However, Isaiah's Haftarah serves as the moral conscience, insisting that ritual purity is useless if it is not matched by ethical action—feeding the hungry, clothing the naked, and freeing the oppressed. True atonement requires repairing both our relationship with God and the brokenness in the world.

Sukkot 1 - Shabbat.nameMeaning: Sukkot (סֻכּוֹת) means 'Booths' or 'Tabernacles'. This reading is for when the first day falls on Shabbat.
Sukkot 1 - Shabbat.context: Sukkot is the 'Season of our Rejoicing', a harvest festival commemorating the miraculous clouds of glory and the fragile huts the Israelites lived in during the Exodus.
Sukkot 1 - Shabbat.summary: Main Torah Reading (Leviticus 22:26-23:44): Outlines the festival cycle, emphasizing the commands to dwell in the Sukkah and take the Four Species. Maftir (Numbers 29:12-16): Lists the massive holiday sacrifices. Haftarah (Zechariah 14:1-21): Envisions a Messianic future where all nations will come to Jerusalem to celebrate Sukkot.
Sukkot 1 - Shabbat.significance: Sukkot combines absolute physical vulnerability (living in a temporary hut) with absolute joy. The Torah reading anchors us in the commandments, while Zechariah's Haftarah reveals Sukkot as the most universal of Jewish holidays, looking forward to an era of global peace. The massive Temple sacrifices, traditionally offered on behalf of the 70 nations of the world, underscore this theme of universal blessing and coexistence.

Sukkot 1 [and 2].nameMeaning: The First and Second Days of Sukkot.
Sukkot 1 [and 2].context: In the Diaspora, the first two days are observed as full Yom Tov (festivals).
Sukkot 1 [and 2].summary: Main Torah Reading (Leviticus 22:26-23:44): Outlines the biblical festival cycle and the specific commandments of Sukkot. Maftir (Numbers 29:12-16): Details the first day's sacrifices. Haftarah (1 Kings 8:2-21): Recounts how King Solomon chose the festival of Sukkot to officially dedicate the First Temple in Jerusalem.
Sukkot 1 [and 2].significance: The Haftarah draws a brilliant parallel between the fragile, temporary Sukkah in the wilderness and the magnificent, permanent Temple built by Solomon. By bringing the Ark into the Holy of Holies during Sukkot, the text teaches that God's presence can dwell just as powerfully in a temporary, vulnerable hut as it can in a grand golden palace, so long as the people make space for Him with joy.

Sukkot Chol Hamoed 1.nameMeaning: The First Intermediate Day of Sukkot.
Sukkot Chol Hamoed 1.context: During the intermediate days of Sukkot, the Torah readings focus entirely on the highly unique, shifting sequence of daily sacrifices brought in the Temple.
Sukkot Chol Hamoed 1.summary: Torah Reading (Numbers 29:17-25): Outlines the daily sacrifices. Uniquely on Sukkot, the number of bulls offered decreases each day (starting from 13 on the first day, down to 7 on the seventh day).
Sukkot Chol Hamoed 1.significance: The total number of bulls offered over the week of Sukkot is exactly 70. According to the Talmud, these were offered to bring atonement, peace, and rain for the '70 nations of the world.' The decreasing number symbolizes the gradual reduction of the world's hostility and idolatry, pointing toward ultimate global harmony.

Sukkot Chol Hamoed 2.nameMeaning: The Second Intermediate Day of Sukkot.
Sukkot Chol Hamoed 2.context: The intermediate days balance the joy of the festival with the solemn daily Temple rites.
Sukkot Chol Hamoed 2.summary: Torah Reading (Numbers 29:20-28): Continues the precise count of the daily sacrifices for the intermediate days of the festival.
Sukkot Chol Hamoed 2.significance: The repetition of these sacrifices underscores the agricultural aspect of Sukkot. It is the time of the final harvest, but also the time when the world is 'judged for water.' The sacrifices were accompanied by the joyous Water Drawing Ceremony, teaching that joy and gratitude are the prerequisites for future blessings.

Sukkot Chol Hamoed 3.nameMeaning: The Third Intermediate Day of Sukkot.
Sukkot Chol Hamoed 3.context: The festival continues, with the daily offerings acting as a countdown through the week.
Sukkot Chol Hamoed 3.summary: Torah Reading (Numbers 29:23-31): Continues the count of the daily sacrifices for the intermediate days of the festival.
Sukkot Chol Hamoed 3.significance: The meticulous daily accounting of the sacrifices reminds the people that even in the midst of a week-long celebration, precision, dedication, and service to God must not be neglected.

Sukkot Chol Hamoed 4.nameMeaning: The Fourth Intermediate Day of Sukkot.
Sukkot Chol Hamoed 4.context: The final intermediate day before the culmination of the festival.
Sukkot Chol Hamoed 4.summary: Torah Reading (Numbers 29:26-34): Continues the count of the daily sacrifices for the intermediate days of the festival.
Sukkot Chol Hamoed 4.significance: As the number of sacrificed bulls decreases, the intensity of the holiday increases, building toward the spiritual climax of Hosha'ana Rabba and Shemini Atzeret.

Hosha'ana Rabba.nameMeaning: Hosha'ana Rabba (הוֹשַׁעְנָא רַבָּא) means 'The Great Salvation' or 'The Great Supplication'.
Hosha'ana Rabba.context: The seventh and final day of Sukkot. It has the atmosphere of a mini-Yom Kippur, viewed mystically as the day the divine judgment written on Rosh Hashanah is finally sealed and delivered.
Hosha'ana Rabba.summary: Torah Reading (Numbers 29:26-34): Outlines the sacrifices for the final days of Sukkot. The day is marked by circling the synagogue seven times with the Four Species and beating willow branches against the floor.
Hosha'ana Rabba.significance: Hosha'ana Rabba is the desperate, final plea for water and life for the coming year. The beating of the willows (which require the most water to survive) symbolizes human fragility and utter dependence on God's mercy and sustenance.

Shemini Atzeret - Shabbat.nameMeaning: Shemini Atzeret (שְׁמִינִי עֲצֶרֶת) means 'The Eighth Day of Assembly'.
Shemini Atzeret - Shabbat.context: Although it immediately follows Sukkot, Shemini Atzeret is an independent holiday. It is an intimate 'after-party' for the Jewish people and God following the universal focus of Sukkot.
Shemini Atzeret - Shabbat.summary: Main Torah Reading (Deuteronomy 14:22-16:17): Reviews the laws of tithing and the Pilgrimage Festivals, commanding the people to be 'only joyful'. Maftir (Numbers 29:35-30:1): Describes the day's sacrifices, noting only *one* bull is offered. Haftarah (1 Kings 8:54-66): Describes King Solomon blessing the nation at the conclusion of the Sukkot dedication.
Shemini Atzeret - Shabbat.significance: After sacrificing 70 bulls for the nations of the world on Sukkot, God asks Israel to stay one more day and offer just one bull (as detailed in the Maftir). The Midrash compares this to a king who hosts a massive banquet for the public, but then asks his closest friend to stay behind for a private, intimate meal. The Haftarah completes this by showing Solomon joyfully blessing the people and sending them home, representing the unique, unbreakable bond between God and the Jewish people.

Simchat Torah.nameMeaning: Simchat Torah (שִׂמְחַת תּוֹרָה) means 'Rejoicing of the Torah'.
Simchat Torah.context: The joyous climax of the autumn holiday season, marking the completion of the annual cycle of Torah readings and its immediate restart.
Simchat Torah.summary: Main Torah Reading (Deuteronomy 33:1-34:12 & Genesis 1:1-2:3): Contains Moses' final blessings and death, immediately followed by restarting the creation story. Maftir (Numbers 29:35-30:1): Details the sacrifices. Haftarah (Joshua 1:1-18): Details God's command to Joshua to lead the people into the Promised Land.
Simchat Torah.significance: Simchat Torah embodies the eternity of Jewish learning. By ending the Torah (Deuteronomy) and instantly restarting it (Genesis) in the same reading, we demonstrate that Torah study is a circle with no end. The Haftarah brilliantly links to the end of the Torah reading: as Moses dies in the Torah, Joshua assumes leadership in the Haftarah. This transition shows that while individual leaders are mortal, the covenant, the Torah, and the mission of the Jewish people are immortal.

Chanukah 1.context: Chanukah commemorates the Maccabean victory over the Syrian-Greeks and the re-dedication of the defiled Second Temple, symbolized by the miracle of the oil lasting eight days.
Chanukah 1.summary: Torah Reading (Numbers 7:1-17): Details the offerings brought by the tribal princes (Nesi'im) during the original dedication of the Tabernacle in the desert.
Chanukah 1.significance: By reading about the dedication of the desert Tabernacle during the festival of Chanukah, the Torah directly links the ancient, pure origins of Jewish worship to the Maccabees' fierce, bloody battle to restore that purity centuries later. It teaches that the spirit of dedication transcends time.

Chanukah 2.context: The readings continue the progressive, daily account of the tribal leaders' offerings.
Chanukah 2.summary: Torah Reading (Numbers 7:18-29): Continues the enumeration of the identical dedication offerings brought by each respective tribe's leader.
Chanukah 2.significance: Even though every tribe brought the exact same offering, the Torah details each one individually. This teaches that God values the unique intention and heart of the giver, not just the physical value of the gift. The progressive lighting of the Menorah mirrors this daily, cumulative dedication.

Chanukah 3.context: The daily readings highlight the unified effort of all the tribes in establishing the sanctuary.
Chanukah 3.summary: Torah Reading (Numbers 7:24-35): Continues the enumeration of the identical dedication offerings brought by each respective tribe's leader.
Chanukah 3.significance: The repetition emphasizes unity and equality. In building a space for holiness, no tribe's contribution was elevated above another's. The Chanukah lights similarly require unity, shining out into the darkness to proclaim a shared miracle.

Chanukah 4.context: The midway point of the festival of lights.
Chanukah 4.summary: Torah Reading (Numbers 7:30-41): Continues the enumeration of the identical dedication offerings brought by each respective tribe's leader.
Chanukah 4.significance: The continuous daily readings build a rhythm of dedication. It reminds us that spiritual renewal (like the re-dedication of the Temple) is not a one-time event, but a steady, deliberate, and sustained effort.

Chanukah 5.context: The light of the Menorah is now officially greater than the darkness (5 out of 8 candles are lit).
Chanukah 5.summary: Torah Reading (Numbers 7:36-47): Continues the enumeration of the identical dedication offerings brought by each respective tribe's leader.
Chanukah 5.significance: The dedication of the altar in the desert was a moment of profound spiritual joy. The Maccabees fought to reclaim that exact joy. The fifth day represents the tipping point where light overpowers the darkness.

Chanukah 6 - Rosh Chodesh.nameMeaning: The Sixth Day of Chanukah, coinciding with Rosh Chodesh (The New Moon).
Chanukah 6 - Rosh Chodesh.context: This is a rare and uniquely holy day where three distinct cycles of time intersect: the weekly Shabbat, the monthly Rosh Chodesh, and the annual festival of Chanukah.
Chanukah 6 - Rosh Chodesh.summary: First Torah (Genesis 41:1-44:17): The regular weekly portion (Mikeitz). Second Torah (Numbers 28:9-15): The Maftir for Rosh Chodesh. Third Torah (Numbers 7:42-47): The Chanukah dedication reading. Haftarah (Zechariah 2:14-4:7; Isaiah 66:1, 23-24; 1 Samuel 20:18, 42): Features Zechariah's famous vision of a solid gold Menorah.
Chanukah 6 - Rosh Chodesh.significance: This rare convergence requires three Torah scrolls, representing weekly, monthly, and annual cycles of holiness. The Haftarah is deeply significant: Zechariah's vision contains the ultimate philosophical message of Chanukah: 'Not by might, nor by power, but by My spirit, says the Lord.' It teaches that while the Maccabees fought a physical war, their ultimate victory and the survival of the Jewish people rely entirely on spiritual resilience and divine light.

Chanukah 7 - Rosh Chodesh.nameMeaning: The Seventh Day of Chanukah, coinciding with Rosh Chodesh.
Chanukah 7 - Rosh Chodesh.context: The intersection of the New Moon and the festival of lights continues.
Chanukah 7 - Rosh Chodesh.summary: First Torah Reading (Numbers 28:1-15): Describes the Rosh Chodesh sacrifices. Second Torah Reading (Numbers 7:48-53): Details the ongoing Chanukah dedication offerings.
Chanukah 7 - Rosh Chodesh.significance: Rosh Chodesh represents renewal and the cyclical nature of time. By overlapping with Chanukah, it reinforces the message that the light of the Torah and the dedication of the Jewish people are constantly renewing, even in the darkest months of winter.

Chanukah 8.nameMeaning: Zot Chanukah (זֹאת חֲנֻכָּה), The Eighth Day of Chanukah.
Chanukah 8.context: The culmination of the festival, where the Menorah is fully ablaze.
Chanukah 8.summary: Torah Reading (Numbers 7:54-8:4): Concludes the dedication offerings of the princes and flows seamlessly into God commanding Aaron the High Priest to light the Menorah in the Tabernacle.
Chanukah 8.significance: The Torah transitions directly from the princes' gifts to Aaron's lighting of the Menorah. The Midrash explains that Aaron felt excluded from the dedication, but God comforted him by saying, 'Your portion is greater than theirs, for you will kindle and prepare the lamps.' The physical gifts of the princes were temporary, but the light of the Menorah (and the Chanukah lights it inspired) is eternal.

Purim.nameMeaning: Purim (פּוּרִים) means 'Lots', referring to the lottery Haman cast to determine the date of the Jews' destruction.
Purim.context: Purim celebrates the miraculous deliverance of the Jewish people in the Persian Empire from Haman's plot to annihilate them.
Purim.summary: Torah Reading (Exodus 17:8-16): Recounts the unprovoked, cowardly attack by the nation of Amalek against the weak and tired Israelites in the desert after the Exodus.
Purim.significance: Haman, the villain of the Purim story, is a direct descendant of Agag, the King of Amalek. The Torah commands the Jews to 'blot out the memory of Amalek.' Amalek represents pure, irrational, unprovoked anti-Semitism. By reading this portion, we connect the specific crisis of the Book of Esther to the eternal, generational struggle against those who seek to destroy the Jewish people without cause.

Shavuot Day 1.nameMeaning: Shavuot (שָׁבוּעוֹת) means 'Weeks', celebrated exactly seven weeks after Passover.
Shavuot Day 1.context: Shavuot is the 'Time of the Giving of our Torah', commemorating the awe-inspiring national revelation at Mount Sinai.
Shavuot Day 1.summary: Main Torah Reading (Exodus 19:1-20:23): The dramatic narrative of the Israelites arriving at Mount Sinai and hearing the Ten Commandments directly from God. Maftir (Numbers 28:26-31): Details the Shavuot sacrifices. Haftarah (Ezekiel 1:1-28; 3:12): The prophet's complex, mystical vision of the Divine Chariot (Ma'aseh Merkavah).
Shavuot Day 1.significance: The Torah reading is the core of Shavuot, marking the exact moment the Israelites transformed into a covenantal nation bound by a moral code. The Maftir grounds us in the agricultural reality of the First Fruits. The Haftarah is chosen for its breathtaking depiction of God's glory: Ezekiel's terrifying and transcendent vision of the Divine Chariot parallels the earth-shattering, fiery revelation the Israelites experienced at Mount Sinai, teaching that receiving the Torah was a deeply mystical, world-altering encounter.

Shavuot Day 2, Shabbat.context: The second day grounds the spiritual heights of the Sinai revelation into the practical, everyday reality of building a society.
Shavuot Day 2, Shabbat.summary: Main Torah Reading (Deuteronomy 14:22-16:17): Outlines the laws of tithes, charity, the Sabbatical year, and the Pilgrimage Festivals. Maftir (Numbers 28:26-31): Details the Shavuot sacrifices. Haftarah (Habakkuk 2:20-3:19): Describes a terrifying and awe-inspiring vision of God's power.
Shavuot Day 2, Shabbat.significance: It is no accident that the Torah reading pairs the Ten Commandments from Day 1 with agricultural laws and charity on Day 2. The spiritual high of receiving the Torah is meaningless unless it translates into a society that cares for the poor, the widow, and the orphan. Habakkuk's vision in the Haftarah serves as a prophetic echo of the thunders and lightning of Mount Sinai, reminding us of the immense power behind these ethical commands.
